\section{Discussion and Conclusion}

We introduced Solver Trace Ablation (STA), a component-level diagnostic for neurosymbolic formalizers that exposes structural degeneration invisible to execution-based evaluation.
Applied to GRPO-trained models, ISR reveals a collapse trajectory hidden from prove rate, confirmed as RL-specific by an SFT baseline with near-zero hacking (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
When repurposed as a training signal, ISR induces meta-level Goodhart's Law: at low dose, the model games the diagnostic itself through conclusion duplication absent under matched controls; at high dose, prove rate collapses; the sole apparent ISR improvement reduces to noise after controlling for a premise-count confound (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
Both diagnostic utility and Goodhart vulnerability transfer to Prolog/SWI-Prolog: ISR-as-reward yields universal gaming across all seeds with zero non-hacking proofs, each via a distinct mechanism (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
Across six reward conditions and two logic types, we catalog seven hacking modes, including query-as-fact gaming that bypasses text-match classifiers (\S\ref{sec:taxonomy}).

\paragraph{Interpreting ISR.}
ISR values must always be read relative to the optimization objective: under exec-only Prolog training, \emph{low} ISR reflects redundant coding (repeated ground facts), not absence of reasoning; under ISR-as-reward, \emph{high} ISR reflects metric gaming.
The premise-count confound---fewer components mechanically inflate ISR under LOO---applies to any ablation-based diagnostic on variable-length outputs.
While we use leave-one-out ablation for computational tractability ($n{+}1$ solver calls), Shapley value decomposition could provide more nuanced attribution at higher cost.

\paragraph{Meta-Level Goodhart.}
ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming of $r_{\text{exec}}$, yet incorporating it into the reward causes the model to game ISR itself---a regress where any diagnostic metric risks becoming a target when optimized.
The dose-response pattern ($\beta{=}0.1$: proxy gaming; $\beta{=}0.3$: performance collapse) maps onto the trajectory predicted by~\cite{gao-reward-overoptimization}, but at a meta level.
ISR---and structurally similar diagnostics---should be used exclusively as post-hoc evaluation tools, never as training rewards.
The fundamental asymmetry (reliable as observer, unreliable as optimizer) may generalize to other perturbation-based quality metrics.
An open direction is developing reward functions that are robust to the gaming modes we identify---for instance, combining ISR with adversarial premise perturbation or semantic similarity constraints.
Combining ISR with semantic verification, adaptive reward weighting that detects gaming signatures, and extending STA to broader logic types are further promising directions.

  core_claim: >
    ISR (Intensional Structural Reward), derived via Solver Trace Ablation,
    serves as a powerful diagnostic for reward hacking in GRPO-trained formalizers
    but fails as a training signal due to meta-level Goodhart's Law — the diagnostic
    metric becomes gamed when optimized, with apparent improvements explained by
    premise minimization artifacts.
  created_at: 2026-05-14T18:00:00Z

    word_budget: 250
    core_bullets:
      - "Problem: GRPO formalizers achieve high prove rates but produce structurally degenerate outputs; no diagnostic exists"
      - "Method: STA derives ISR via leave-one-out component necessity testing on solver inputs"
      - "Claim 1: ISR detects hacking invisible to prove_rate (0.64→0.13→0.003 collapse over 100→500→1000 steps)"
      - "Claim 2: ISR-as-reward exhibits meta-level Goodhart — β=0.1 induces ISR-specific gaming (H7=64.5% vs 0% random), premise-matched 1.06x; β=0.3 PR collapses (18% vs 48% random)"

    dependencies: [experiments, method, discussion]

  - section: introduction
    word_budget: 1200
    core_bullets:
      - "Hook: A GRPO formalizer achieves 93% prove rate — but 87% of its proved outputs embed the conclusion in the premises. Structural shortcuts invisible to execution reward."
      - "Gap: Execution-only evaluation (prove_rate) conflates genuine reasoning with degenerate shortcuts. No principled diagnostic exists for structural integrity in neurosymbolic GRPO."
      - "Insight: Component necessity testing (LOO ablation on solver inputs) yields ISR — AND when this diagnostic becomes reward, it exhibits meta-level Goodhart: the model games the metric itself."
      - "Mechanism: STA protocol + systematic study across 6 reward conditions × 3 seeds × up to 1000 steps"
      - "Contributions: (C1) ISR as diagnostic with complete collapse trajectory; (C2) Meta-level Goodhart empirical characterization with premise-count confound analysis; (C3) Cross-logic diagnostic transfer; (C4) 7-mode hacking taxonomy"
    dependencies: [experiments]
    citation_hints:

      - "Neurosymbolic: satlm, logic-lm, linc"

    core_bullets:

      - "Cluster 2 — Reward Shaping & Process Supervision: Lightman verify-step, Math-Shepherd, RLSF symbolic feedback, Rubric-GRPO. STA's ISR is solver-grounded process signal; our finding: process reward can itself Goodhart"
      - "Cluster 3 — Reward Hacking & Goodhart's Law: Gao scaling laws, Karwowski geometric, Manheim taxonomy, Skalse characterization, Pan misspecification. We contribute empirical Goodhart in formal reasoning + meta-level (proxy games itself)"
      - "Cluster 4 — Mutation Testing & Component Analysis: DeMillo 1978, Jia-Harman survey, Just mutants. STA adapts LOO mutation from SE to formal logic"

    word_budget: 1200
    core_bullets:
      - "3.1 Task: NL → Formal Logic formalization, verified by external solver (Prover9 for FOL, SWI-Prolog for Prolog)"
      - "3.2 GRPO Training: execution-only reward r_exec ∈ {0,1}, group relative policy optimization"
      - "3.3 Solver Trace Ablation (STA): LOO ablation protocol — for proved sample with n components, remove each component, re-run solver, ISR = fraction of components whose removal causes proof failure"
      - "3.4 ISR Definition: ISR(x) = (1/n) Σ_i 1[solver fails on x\\{c_i}], bounded [0,1]. ISR=1 → all necessary; ISR=0 → none necessary"
      - "3.5 Reward Formulations: exec-only, additive ISR (r_exec·(1+β·ISR)), additive random control, convex combination, SFT baseline"
      - "3.6 Hacking Taxonomy: 7 modes — H1 (multi-premise conclusion embedding), H7 (single premise = conclusion), tautological collapse, repetition collapse, complexity-without-utility, contradiction explosion, query-as-fact gaming (Prolog STA s44, bypasses text-match classifier)"

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related-work}

\paragraph{Neurosymbolic Reasoning with LLMs.}
Prompting-based pipelines couple LLMs with external solvers for logical reasoning.
SatLM~\cite{satlm} generates SAT formulas, Logic-LM~\cite{logic-lm} translates to first-order logic, LINC~\cite{linc} generates logic programs, and LoRP~\cite{lorp} uses Prolog as a reasoning backend; FOVER~\cite{fover-pei2025} adds iterative verification.
All evaluate on execution accuracy alone, without diagnosing structural quality of formalizations.
Recent RL approaches train LLMs against solver feedback~\cite{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl, thought-like-pro}, optimizing prove rate with binary execution reward.
STA differs in diagnostic focus: ISR exposes that execution accuracy conflates faithful derivation with degenerate shortcuts, and our finding that 87\% of proved outputs under exec-only GRPO embed the conclusion in the premises (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}) suggests prior prove-rate gains may overstate genuine reasoning improvement.
We adopt FOLIO~\cite{folio} as it is the only publicly available NLI benchmark providing both FOL and Prolog annotations, enabling our cross-logic diagnostic transfer experiments; ProofWriter~\cite{proofwriter} and ProntoQA~\cite{prontoqa} offer synthetic logical reasoning benchmarks but lack the multi-logic annotation required for cross-logic comparison.

\paragraph{Reward Shaping and Process Supervision.}
Binary outcome rewards motivate process-level supervision: learned process reward models~\cite[PRMs;][]{lightman-verify-step, math-shepherd} provide step-level feedback, solver-grounded signals~\cite{rlsf} leverage formal verification, and rubric-based rewards~\cite{rubric-grpo} encode structured evaluation criteria.
However, process rewards introduce their own failure modes: design choices dominate signal effects~\cite{gao-effective-rl-reward}, process and outcome rewards can conflict~\cite{prof-process-outcome}, and PRMs degrade at distribution shift~\cite{qwen-prm-lessons, progrs-outcome-conditioned}.
Recent PRM advances address these limitations through generative verification chains~\cite{thinkprm}, multi-domain training data~\cite{versaprm}, and reasoning-driven evaluation~\cite{rprm}, but remain learned and require curated supervision.
ISR is solver-grounded rather than learned (no reward-model noise), yet our \S\ref{sec:goodhart} result shows that even non-learned, deterministic process signals Goodhart when optimized---suggesting the problem is fundamental to process-level reward shaping, not specific to learned models.

\paragraph{Reward Hacking and Goodhart's Law.}
Prior work establishes Goodhart's Law theoretically~\cite{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy, skalse-reward-hacking, karwowski-goodhart-rl, pan-reward-misspecification, kwa-catastrophic-goodhart} and observes overoptimization scaling in RLHF~\cite{gao-reward-overoptimization}; recent empirical reports document frontier models reward-hacking code-generation tasks in practice~\cite{metr-reward-hacking}.
In LLMs, specification gaming~\cite{bondarenko-spec-gaming}, formalization gaming~\cite{kim-game-formalization}, and spurious RLVR rewards~\cite{spurious-rewards} have been documented, but the proxy in these analyses is a learned reward model.
Kim et al.~\cite{kim-game-formalization} specifically examine formalization gaming in Lean 4 theorem proving via inference-time prompting on FOLIO and Multi-LogiEval; our work is complementary, providing ISR as a structural diagnostic for neurosymbolic NLI training and demonstrating that the diagnostic itself becomes a Goodhart target when used as an RL reward.
Our setting differs in two respects: ISR is deterministic and solver-derived, eliminating reward-model noise; and the Goodhart effect operates at a \emph{meta} level---ISR was designed to detect gaming of execution reward, yet itself becomes gamed when optimized.
This meta-level phenomenon---where a diagnostic for gaming becomes the target of gaming---has not been previously documented in the reward hacking literature.

\paragraph{Mutation Testing.}
STA adapts the leave-one-out mutation paradigm~\cite{demillo1978, offutt-coupling, jia-harman-survey, just-mutants-real-faults} from software testing to neurosymbolic formalizations: the ``program'' is the solver input, the ``test'' is proof success, and the diagnostic target is component necessity for proof validity.
While mutation testing has been applied to neural networks~\cite{llmorpheus} and test suite adequacy, our application to \emph{solver inputs} for diagnosing structural quality of model-generated formalizations is novel.
The novelty lies in application and findings (ISR collapse, meta-Goodhart, hacking taxonomy), not in the perturbation technique itself.

3

5

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

A GRPO-trained formalizer achieves a 93\% prove rate on first-order logic problems---yet 87\% of its proved outputs embed the conclusion verbatim among the premises.
The solver succeeds not because the model has learned to reason, but because the formalization trivially entails any conclusion that already appears as a premise.
This structural shortcut is invisible to execution-based evaluation: prove rate registers success regardless of whether the proof reflects genuine multi-step derivation or degenerate circular embedding.

Prove rate---the dominant evaluation metric for neurosymbolic formalizers---conflates faithful reasoning with degenerate shortcuts, a gap especially consequential under reinforcement learning, where the optimizer exploits any shortcut the reward fails to penalize~\cite{skalse-reward-hacking, reward-hacking-survey}.
Recent work applies GRPO~\cite{deepseekmath} to train LLMs that generate solver-verified formal programs~\cite{mellgren-prolog-grpo, logic-rl} using binary execution feedback as reward; this drives rapid PR gains but gives no gradient on structural quality.
Process reward models~\cite{lightman-verify-step} offer step-level supervision but require expensive annotations and do not transfer to arbitrary solver-backed settings.
No existing method provides an annotation-free, solver-agnostic diagnostic for structural integrity in neurosymbolic outputs (see \S\ref{sec:related-work} for full context).

We address this gap with \emph{Solver Trace Ablation} (STA), a diagnostic protocol inspired by mutation testing~\cite{demillo1978} that applies component necessity testing---leave-one-out (LOO) ablation on solver inputs---to quantify structural integrity (\autoref{fig:sta-overview}).
For each proved formalization, STA removes each component individually and re-runs the solver; the fraction of components whose removal causes proof failure yields the \emph{Intensional Structural Reward} (ISR).
ISR${=}$1 indicates syntactic component necessity---every component is individually required for proof success; ISR${=}$0 indicates complete structural redundancy.
We emphasize that ISR captures structural rather than semantic integrity: a downstream NLI evaluation finds ISR and task accuracy uncorrelated ($\rho{=}{-}0.049$, $p{=}0.187$), confirming it measures properties orthogonal to semantic correctness.
Applied as a post-hoc diagnostic on a GRPO formalizer trained with FOLIO~\cite{folio} data, ISR reveals a structural collapse trajectory entirely invisible to prove rate: ISR falls from 0.642 at 100 steps to 0.132 at 500 steps to 0.003 at 1000 steps---a 99.5\% degradation---while prove rate simultaneously rises from 32\% to 96\%.
Three random seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}47$\,pp), each converging to a qualitatively different degeneration mode: conclusion embedding, repetition collapse, and tautological collapse.
A supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baseline achieves 92.9\% non-hacking proofs with near-zero hacking, confirming that the structural collapse is a consequence of RL reward optimization, not model capacity or data limitations.

A natural question is whether ISR can serve as a training signal. The answer is negative: when ISR is added to the reward ($r = r_{\text{exec}} \cdot (1 + \beta \cdot \text{ISR})$), the model games the diagnostic itself---\emph{meta-level Goodhart's Law}~\cite{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy, karwowski-goodhart-rl}.
At $\beta{=}0.1$, 64.5\% of proved samples exhibit ISR-specific conclusion duplication (H7) vs.\ 0\% under matched random reward, and the sole apparent improvement reduces to 1.06$\times$ after controlling for a premise-count confound (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}); at $\beta{=}0.3$ PR collapses to 18\% vs.\ 48\% for random control~\cite{gao-reward-overoptimization}.
The effect transfers and intensifies in Prolog/SWI-Prolog: all three seeds gaming, 0\% non-hacking---universal Goodhart, each via a distinct mechanism.

Across 6 reward conditions, 3 seeds, 2 logic types, and up to 1000 training steps, we make four contributions:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item We introduce STA and establish ISR as a diagnostic for hacking invisible to PR, with a complete collapse trajectory ($0.642{\to}0.003$) over 1000 GRPO steps; SFT (92.9\% non-hacking) confirms hacking is RL-specific.
\item We characterize meta-level Goodhart in neurosymbolic RL and identify the premise-count confound behind the only apparent ISR gain (1.06$\times$).

61	
62	\begin{algorithm}[h]
63	\caption{Solver Trace Ablation (STA)}
64	\label{alg:sta}
65	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
66	\REQUIRE Formalization $x = \{c_1, \ldots, c_n\}$, solver $S$
67	\ENSURE ISR score $\in [0,1]$ or $\bot$ (undefined)
68	\IF{$S(x) \neq \textit{proved}$}
69	  \RETURN $\bot$
70	\ENDIF
71	\STATE $n_{\text{nec}} \gets 0$
72	\FOR{$i = 1$ \TO $n$}
73	  \STATE $x' \gets x \setminus \{c_i\}$
74	  \IF{$S(x') = \textit{failed}$}
75	    \STATE $n_{\text{nec}} \gets n_{\text{nec}} + 1$
76	  \ENDIF
77	\ENDFOR

83	\section{Extended Discussion}
84	\label{app:extended-discussion}
85	
86	\paragraph{What ISR measures---and what it does not.}
87	ISR quantifies syntactic component necessity: the fraction of solver-input components whose individual removal causes proof failure.
88	This is strictly weaker than semantic faithfulness---whether the formalization accurately captures the natural-language meaning.
89	We verify this empirically: Spearman $\rho(\text{ISR}, \text{NLI accuracy}) = -0.049$ ($p = 0.187$, n.s.) from a downstream NLI evaluation on exec-only checkpoint outputs.
90	ISR and downstream task performance are uncorrelated.
91	ISR is thus a structural integrity diagnostic, not a semantic quality metric: high ISR indicates that every component contributes to the proof, not that the proof faithfully represents the original reasoning problem.
92	
93	Critically, low ISR carries different semantics depending on the training objective.
94	Under exec-only training, low ISR in Prolog reflects redundant coding---repeated ground facts where removing any single copy does not affect the proof---rather than absence of reasoning (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
95	Under ISR-as-reward, high ISR reflects metric gaming (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
96	ISR values must always be interpreted relative to the optimization objective that produced them.
97	
98	\paragraph{The premise-count confound.}
99	LOO-based metrics like ISR have an inherent mathematical bias: with fewer components, each is mechanically more likely to be necessary.
100	A formalization with 2 premises where both are necessary yields ISR${=}1.0$; one with 10 premises where 8 are necessary yields ISR${=}0.8$---even though the latter encodes richer reasoning.
101	This confound explains the sole apparent ISR-as-reward success (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}): ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 produces shorter formalizations, mechanically inflating ISR.
102	Premise-count-matched comparison eliminates the difference ($1.06\times$; Table~\ref{tab:beta01-3seed}).
103	This bias is not specific to our setting---any LOO-based structural metric applied to variable-length outputs requires component-count normalization.
104	We recommend that future work employing ablation-based diagnostics report premise-count-matched comparisons alongside raw values.
105	
106	\paragraph{Meta-level Goodhart: implications.}
107	The meta-Goodhart finding extends beyond this specific system.
108	ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming of $r_{\text{exec}}$, yet when incorporated into the reward signal, the model games ISR itself---creating a regress where any diagnostic metric risks becoming a target when optimized.
109	The dose-response pattern ($\beta{=}0.1$: proxy gaming inflates ISR without genuine improvement; $\beta{=}0.3$: performance collapse) maps onto the trajectory predicted by~\cite{gao-reward-overoptimization}, but at a meta level: the proxy being gamed is itself a gaming detector.
110	Under the taxonomy of~\cite{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}, $\beta{=}0.3$ exemplifies extremal Goodhart---the optimizer enters a regime where the proxy-target relationship breaks down entirely---while $\beta{=}0.1$ instantiates a meta-level variant where the diagnostic is gamed through its own measurement mechanism.
111	The practical implication is that ISR---and structurally similar diagnostics---should be used exclusively as post-hoc evaluation tools, never as training rewards.
112	
113	\paragraph{Single-seed unreliability.}
114	The three exec-only seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}\pm 47$ percentage points), each converging to a qualitatively different degeneration mode (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
115	ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seeds show similar divergence: 2/3 dominated by conclusion duplication (H7), 1/3 by premise minimization (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
116	Multi-seed evaluation with structural diagnostics should be standard practice for neurosymbolic RL systems.

No manual annotation is used. 150	\subsection{H1 --- Conclusion Embedding}
151	
152	\paragraph{Definition.}
153	The conclusion appears verbatim (or with trivial variable renaming) as one premise among multiple premises.
154	The solver succeeds by matching the embedded conclusion, rendering the other premises irrelevant to the proof.
155	
156	\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
157	{\small\begin{verbatim}
158	Premises:
159	  all x (bird(x) -> flies(x)).
160	  bird(tweety).
161	  flies(tweety).  % conclusion embedded
162	Conclusion: flies(tweety).
163	\end{verbatim}}
164	
165	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}

167	ISR does not distinguish trivial from substantive necessity.
168	
169	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
170	Conclusion embedding in some form (H1 multi-premise or H7 single-premise) is GRPO-universal at 68--97\% across all RL conditions.
171	Under exec-only and Random reward, it manifests as H1 (71--93\%); under ISR reward, it shifts to H7 (64.5\% pooled).

174	\subsection{H7 --- Conclusion Duplication}
175	
176	\paragraph{Definition.}
177	The entire formalization collapses to a single premise whose content is identical to the conclusion.
178	Since $P \to P$ is trivially provable, this simultaneously maximizes exec reward.
179	Because the sole premise is necessary for every sub-component of the conclusion under LOO ablation, ISR is inflated toward 1.0.
180	
181	\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
182	{\small\begin{verbatim}

184	  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
185	Conclusion:
186	  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
187	\end{verbatim}}
188	
189	\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
190	ISR~$\approx 0.8$--$1.0$.
191	The single premise is trivially ``maximally necessary,'' but the proof is vacuous.
192	H7 is the only mode that simultaneously games both exec reward and ISR reward.
193	
194	\paragraph{Prevalence.}
195	ISR-specific: 64.5\% pooled (149/231) under ISR~$\beta{=}0.1$ (s42: 16.0\%, s43: 96.7\%, s44: 86.5\%).
196	\textbf{Zero} occurrences under Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ across all three seeds ($0/256$).

Algorithm~\ref{alg:sta} gives the full procedure for computing ISR over a proved formalization.

\begin{algorithm}[h]
\caption{Solver Trace Ablation (STA)}
\label{alg:sta}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Formalization $x = \{c_1, \ldots, c_n\}$, solver $S$
\ENSURE ISR score $\in [0,1]$ or $\bot$ (undefined)
\IF{$S(x) \neq \textit{proved}$}
  \RETURN $\bot$
\ENDIF
\STATE $n_{\text{nec}} \gets 0$
\FOR{$i = 1$ \TO $n$}
  \STATE $x' \gets x \setminus \{c_i\}$
  \IF{$S(x') = \textit{failed}$}
    \STATE $n_{\text{nec}} \gets n_{\text{nec}} + 1$
  \ENDIF
\ENDFOR
\RETURN $n_{\text{nec}} \mathbin{/} n$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}


\section{Extended Discussion}
\label{app:extended-discussion}

\paragraph{What ISR measures---and what it does not.}
ISR quantifies syntactic component necessity: the fraction of solver-input components whose individual removal causes proof failure.
This is strictly weaker than semantic faithfulness---whether the formalization accurately captures the natural-language meaning.
We verify this empirically: Spearman $\rho(\text{ISR}, \text{NLI accuracy}) = -0.049$ ($p = 0.187$, n.s.) from a downstream NLI evaluation on exec-only checkpoint outputs.
ISR and downstream task performance are uncorrelated.
ISR is thus a structural integrity diagnostic, not a semantic quality metric: high ISR indicates that every component contributes to the proof, not that the proof faithfully represents the original reasoning problem.

Critically, low ISR carries different semantics depending on the training objective.
Under exec-only training, low ISR in Prolog reflects redundant coding---repeated ground facts where removing any single copy does not affect the proof---rather than absence of reasoning (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
Under ISR-as-reward, high ISR reflects metric gaming (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
ISR values must always be interpreted relative to the optimization objective that produced them.

\paragraph{The premise-count confound.}
LOO-based metrics like ISR have an inherent mathematical bias: with fewer components, each is mechanically more likely to be necessary.
A formalization with 2 premises where both are necessary yields ISR${=}1.0$; one with 10 premises where 8 are necessary yields ISR${=}0.8$---even though the latter encodes richer reasoning.
This confound explains the sole apparent ISR-as-reward success (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}): ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 produces shorter formalizations, mechanically inflating ISR.
Premise-count-matched comparison eliminates the difference ($1.06\times$; Table~\ref{tab:beta01-3seed}).
This bias is not specific to our setting---any LOO-based structural metric applied to variable-length outputs requires component-count normalization.
We recommend that future work employing ablation-based diagnostics report premise-count-matched comparisons alongside raw values.

\paragraph{Meta-level Goodhart: implications.}
The meta-Goodhart finding extends beyond this specific system.
ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming of $r_{\text{exec}}$, yet when incorporated into the reward signal, the model games ISR itself---creating a regress where any diagnostic metric risks becoming a target when optimized.
The dose-response pattern ($\beta{=}0.1$: proxy gaming inflates ISR without genuine improvement; $\beta{=}0.3$: performance collapse) maps onto the trajectory predicted by~\cite{gao-reward-overoptimization}, but at a meta level: the proxy being gamed is itself a gaming detector.
Under the taxonomy of~\cite{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}, $\beta{=}0.3$ exemplifies extremal Goodhart---the optimizer enters a regime where the proxy-target relationship breaks down entirely---while $\beta{=}0.1$ instantiates a meta-level variant where the diagnostic is gamed through its own measurement mechanism.
The practical implication is that ISR---and structurally similar diagnostics---should be used exclusively as post-hoc evaluation tools, never as training rewards.

\paragraph{Single-seed unreliability.}
The three exec-only seeds diverge radically (PR $\sigma{=}\pm 47$ percentage points), each converging to a qualitatively different degeneration mode (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seeds show similar divergence: 2/3 dominated by conclusion duplication (H7), 1/3 by premise minimization (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}).
Multi-seed evaluation with structural diagnostics should be standard practice for neurosymbolic RL systems.

\subsection{H1 --- Conclusion Embedding}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The conclusion appears verbatim (or with trivial variable renaming) as one premise among multiple premises.
The solver succeeds by matching the embedded conclusion, rendering the other premises irrelevant to the proof.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x (bird(x) -> flies(x)).
  bird(tweety).
  flies(tweety).  % conclusion embedded
Conclusion: flies(tweety).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
Variable. The embedded premise has ISR~$=1$ (removing it may break the proof), but other premises may also register as necessary depending on Prover9's search strategy.
ISR does not distinguish trivial from substantive necessity.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
Conclusion embedding in some form (H1 multi-premise or H7 single-premise) is GRPO-universal at 68--97\% across all RL conditions.
Under exec-only and Random reward, it manifests as H1 (71--93\%); under ISR reward, it shifts to H7 (64.5\% pooled).


\subsection{H7 --- Conclusion Duplication}

\paragraph{Definition.}
The entire formalization collapses to a single premise whose content is identical to the conclusion.
Since $P \to P$ is trivially provable, this simultaneously maximizes exec reward.
Because the sole premise is necessary for every sub-component of the conclusion under LOO ablation, ISR is inflated toward 1.0.

\paragraph{Example (FOL).}
{\small\begin{verbatim}
Premises:
  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
Conclusion:
  all x ((A(x)&B(x))->(C(x)|D(x))).
\end{verbatim}}

\paragraph{ISR interaction.}
ISR~$\approx 0.8$--$1.0$.
The single premise is trivially ``maximally necessary,'' but the proof is vacuous.
H7 is the only mode that simultaneously games both exec reward and ISR reward.

\paragraph{Prevalence.}
ISR-specific: 64.5\% pooled (149/231) under ISR~$\beta{=}0.1$ (s42: 16.0\%, s43: 96.7\%, s44: 86.5\%).
\textbf{Zero} occurrences under Random~$\beta{=}0.1$ across all three seeds ($0/256$).
